world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Les quatre types sous-jacents attendus dans une langue qui ne comporte que deux tons ponctuels sont identifiés dans le profil tonal du nom suivi d'un numéral, forme dans laquelle le préfixe porte un ton B. Il s'ensuit que le changement de profil pour les autres cas est provoqué par l'introduction d'un ton H sur le préfixe. [...] [p.255:] Ce mécanisme de report est lié au fait que la langue n'admet pas de ton montant.
new_statements.translation: The four underlying types expected in a language that has only two level tones are identified in the tonal profile of the noun followed by a numeral, a form in which the prefix bears a L tone. It follows that the change of profile in the other cases is caused by the introduction of a H tone on the prefix. [...] This transfer mechanism is linked to the fact that the language does not admit a rising tone.
new_statements.citation: Puech, Gilbert. 1988. Augment et préfixe nominal en ngubi. Pholia 3: 247-256. Lyon: Laboratoire de Phonétique et Linguistique Africaine, CRLS, Université Lumière Lyon 2.
new_statements.locator: section 'Les profils tonals', p.254 (first two sentences) and p.255 (last sentence)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (290 pp., text layer, PDF page = printed page; extracted text). Puech, G. 1988 'Augment et prefixe nominal en ngubi', Pholia 3: 247-256. Both quoted passages are present verbatim: p.254, section 'Les profils tonals', immediately after the four-profile table: 'Les quatre types sous-jacents attendus dans une langue qui ne comporte que deux tons ponctuels sont identifies dans le profil tonal du nom suivi d'un numeral, forme dans laquelle le prefixe porte un ton B. Il s'ensuit que le changement de profil pour les autres cas est provoque par l'introduction d'un ton H sur le prefixe.'; p.255, last sentence before 'Conclusion': 'Ce mecanisme de report est lie au fait que la langue n'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ngubi is analysed as a two-level-tone language (H/L with downstep, tonal augment, no rising tones); the source says nothing about word stress or accent. Observation only (not stated by the author): radical vowels of disyllabic stems are written long in utterance-final citation forms and short when a numeral/associative follows (e.g. ímù:sú 'visage' vs ímùsú wá díbáɣàlà), and Blanchon 1990 treats long vs short radical vowels in Ngubi as lexical.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding prominence; tonal detail only (augment H projects onto prefix; L prefix tone shifts onto first radical H creating a downstep; no rising tones allowed).
new_statements.domain_note: Data are isolated citation forms and noun + numeral / associative phrases from two speakers (Idjembo and Odimba, April 1988); no word-level accent domain is defined.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same variety: ngubi = ngove/ngové/ngowe (the Nkomi name), Guthrie-Maho B404 (Pholia 4 labels it 'B 46'), spoken by elderly speakers around the Iguéla (Ngové) lagoon south of Fernan-Vaz; Puech's data come from Idjembo and Odimba (Sainte-Anne). Glottolog ngub1239, no ISO code. Speakers have shifted to Nkomi (Myene B11e). Not to be confused with Ngove as a toponym or with Vungu/'yibungu' (B403).

sources.citation: Puech, Gilbert. 1988. Augment et préfixe nominal en ngubi. Pholia 3: 247-256. Lyon: Laboratoire de Phonétique et Linguistique Africaine, CRLS, Université Lumière Lyon 2.

sources.locator: section 'Les profils tonals', p.254 (first two sentences) and p.255 (last sentence)
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. Tonal analysis only: Ngubi has 'deux tons ponctuels' (H, B) with downstep (p.254), no rising tone (p.255); radical vowels are transcribed long in utterance-final elicitation forms and short when a determiner follows, and the term 'more' (mora) of the radical vowel is used (p.254), but the author never comments on length or prominence.

sources.citation: Van der Veen, Lolke. 2006 / 2007. ALGAB (Atlas Linguistique du Gabon) project papers, DDL Lyon.
sources.note: Ngubi (ŋgubi B404) appears only in the inventory tables; nothing on phonology.

sources.citation: Blanchon, Jean A. 1990. The Great *HL Split in Bantu Group B40. Pholia 5: 17-29.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Uses Puech's Ngubi field notes (fn.6): Ngubi is 'the most conservative of the B40 dialects' and, unlike all other B40 dialects, not a 'tone-case' language (pp.18-19); Ngubi infinitive tone classes depend on whether the stem is polysyllabic or has a long vs short radical vowel (pp.27-28), i.e. radical vowel length treated as lexical. Purely tonal.
